# FlexUltra

FlexUltra is a headless bridge between FLEX inside jailbroken iOS app processes and automation clients such as a CLI or MCP server.

The current implementation contains:

- `FlexUltraAgent.dylib`, injected into UIKit apps. It connects outbound to the broker and dynamically loads FlexUltra's private vendored `libFLEX.dylib` when needed. The Reflex loader remains present for a future safely qualified Swift path but is currently disabled.
- `flexultrad`, a loopback-only broker that tracks injected processes and routes JSON requests.
- `flexultra`, a JSON-first CLI for target discovery, FLEX visibility, FLEX-backed runtime inspection, UIKit discovery/control, screenshots, and bounded Objective-C invocation.
- `flexultra-mcp`, a stdio MCP server exposing the same broker operations directly to AI clients. It opens no additional network listener.

FLEX is vendored into the FlexUltra package as a private runtime at `/var/jb/usr/lib/flexultra/libFLEX.dylib`, so no external `libflex` package is required. FlexUltra also packages its Reflex/Echo helper privately, but current builds use only the safe `FLEXSwiftMetadataInspector` entry point from that helper. Automatic Reflex integration and `FLEXSwiftMirror` stay disabled because mirror construction has crashed tested targets. `swift inspect` / `flexultra_swift_inspect` therefore expose Swift class metadata only and never read live Swift values.

Objective-C message tracing is powered by a vendored copy of [ObjSee for iOS](https://github.com/EthanArbuckle/objsee-ios). FlexUltra wraps ObjSee with bounded, process-scoped trace sessions and JSON/CLI/MCP surfaces intended for AI-driven investigation.

## Build

```sh
make package
```

The current package is rootless and targets iOS 15+ arm64/arm64e devices.

Application discovery/lifecycle commands and physical device input are broker-local operations. `flexultrad` invokes an installed iCLI binary with direct argv execution and passes its JSON result through to CLI/MCP clients. iCLI is runtime-optional and is intentionally not a package dependency; the package dependency is exactly `firmware (>= 15.0)`. When iCLI is unavailable or fails, the broker returns structured dependency errors instead of attempting target routing.

`flexultra targets` is the authoritative broker view of connected injected processes. The daemon is compiled with the expected deterministic agent build fingerprint, and every target is classified with `build_status` (`current`, `stale`, or `unknown`), `current_agent`, `refresh_recommended`, `connected_at_unix_ms`, and `connection_sequence`. Prefer a `current` target for investigation. `flexultra resolve` deterministically resolves an exact PID first, then bundle identifier, then process name; ambiguous bundle/process matches return `target_ambiguous` with candidate metadata. After resolving a name, use the returned PID for subsequent requests.

JSON is the default output. Add `--human` for terminal-friendly output.

`health` is the cheap qualification call for an injected target. It verifies the current process generation, reports the deterministic `agent_build` fingerprint, loads/verifies FLEX on demand, samples UIKit window availability, and reports current experiment/trace/heap state plus the target's live operation support. UIKit sampling is synchronous only while the dedicated heap worker is idle. While heap work is active, `health` stays bounded by returning the most recently cached UIKit sample with `ui.sample_fresh: false` and `ui.sample_deferred_due_to_heap: true`; if no cached sample exists yet, it returns a zero-window placeholder until the next idle call can refresh it. The next idle `health` call samples UIKit again and reports `sample_fresh: true` / `sample_deferred_due_to_heap: false`. `operation_support` contains one entry for every injected-agent operation and reports `supported`, `source`, `requirements`, plus a structured `reason` when unavailable and optional `conditional`/`limitations` metadata when runtime support depends on the selected member or data kind. `supported_operations` and `unsupported_operations` are compact indexes for agents. Use this per-operation map as the authoritative dispatch gate; `capabilities` and `flex.features` remain broad compatibility summaries. Current builds expose the safe Swift metadata path with `capabilities.swift_inspection=true`, `capabilities.swift_value_inspection=false`, and `flex.features.swift_metadata=true`. `flex.features.swift_mirror=false` and `flex.features.reflex=false` remain deliberate: `FLEXObjectExplorer` automatic Reflex integration stays disabled, and FlexUltra never constructs `FLEXSwiftMirror`. `healthy` means the agent is responsive, the process generation stayed consistent, FLEX is available, and the reported UIKit sample contains at least one window. A key window is reported separately and is not required for `healthy`.

For AI-driven inspection, `investigate screen` is the recommended first call. It captures the current UIKit snapshot, chooses a useful visible focus automatically, deep-inspects that object through UIKit + FLEX, and returns bounded suggested next actions in one response. An explicit live handle or stable UIKit selector can be supplied when the caller already knows what to focus; otherwise `focus_source` is `auto_snapshot`. The aggregate also attempts the safe Swift metadata-only inspector for the focus. That section may include class-descriptor/field metadata, but it always suppresses live Swift values and never invokes `FLEXSwiftMirror`. Image-enabled results keep the screenshot payload only at the top level, so MCP emits exactly one image while the nested snapshot remains JSON-friendly.

`investigate element` is the tweak-development follow-up after a screen pass identifies the UI object that matters. It is read-only and structured-only. In one request it combines the selected element's deep UIKit/FLEX state, `object inspect`, exact runtime class plus methods/properties/ivars, a bounded reverse-reference graph, stable selector, related runtime class candidates, evidence-backed target/action hook candidates, and an optional bounded ObjSee trace recipe. Hook selectors are emitted only when UIKit/FLEX observed them on a control or gesture target/action; related controller/responder/superview/reference classes stay as class candidates and are never converted into guessed selectors. The aggregate runs on the dedicated heap worker because reference-graph discovery can be expensive. If that optional graph exceeds its heap time budget, the rest of the investigation still succeeds, `reference_graph` reports the structured `heap_timeout`, and `next_actions` includes a smaller bounded `heap.reference_graph` retry.

`ui snapshot-save` and `ui snapshot-diff` let an AI compare UIKit state across an action without retaining screenshots or live object handles. A saved baseline stores compact JSON-safe element state only, is scoped to the current target process generation, and receives an ID such as `snap_<generation>_<counter>`. FlexUltra retains at most eight saved baselines per process. `snapshot-diff` compares a fresh snapshot against that baseline and returns bounded `added`, `removed`, `moved`, and `changed` collections plus counts and truncation metadata. If `--root` or `--max-nodes` are omitted, the baseline capture settings are reused. `--max-changes` defaults to 200 and accepts 1–1000 entries per category. A baseline from an earlier process generation returns `stale_snapshot`; an unknown or evicted current-generation ID returns `snapshot_not_found`.

Every `object.*` command accepts either a process-scoped handle or a stable UIKit selector returned by `ui find` / `ui snapshot`. Selector targets are resolved inside the object operation immediately before FLEX inspection, so AI clients can keep a semantic target across redraws and app relaunches without first calling `ui resolve`. Selector-backed results report `target_source: "ui_selector"` and `resolved_by`; `--root`, `--max-nodes`, and `--include-hidden` control resolution. Focused object queries are paged with `--offset` and `--limit`. Property, ivar, and method lists accept `--query <text>` for server-side case-insensitive filtering before pagination, keeping large FLEX surfaces token-efficient for AI clients. Each `object methods` entry includes machine-readable `invocation` metadata with `callable`, the explicit argument count, and normalized argument/return JSON shapes derived from the same ABI rules as `object call`; nil-only block parameters are identified explicitly. Property and ivar queries also accept `--no-values`. `object get` and `object set` accept `--kind auto|property|ivar`; `auto` resolves a property before an ivar with the same name.

`swift inspect` performs safe metadata-only Swift inspection through `FLEXSwiftMetadataInspector`. Successful results report `source: "FLEXSwiftMetadataInspector"`, `mode: "metadata_only"`, `include_values: false`, and `swift_values_available: false`. If a caller requests values, FlexUltra still returns metadata only and adds `value_suppression_reason: "metadata_only_safe_mode"`. Live Swift field values, writes, mangled-type resolution, protocol-conformance enumeration, automatic Reflex integration, and `FLEXSwiftMirror` remain disabled because installed-device testing showed the mirror path can terminate tested targets.

`object set` accepts JSON scalars plus existing object handles for object-valued properties and ivars. Use a generation-qualified handle such as `@obj_0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef_43` in the CLI or `{"handle":"obj_0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef_43"}` in protocol/MCP requests. A handle from a previous target process generation returns `stale_handle` with both `handle_generation` and `current_generation`; an unknown or deallocated handle from the current generation returns `object_not_found`. Object handles are rejected for primitive members. Bare values that are not valid JSON syntax are treated as strings by the CLI.

`object call` uses Objective-C method signatures and supports object, `Class`, `SEL`, boolean/integer/floating-point primitives, `CGPoint`, `CGSize`, `CGRect`, `UIEdgeInsets`, `NSRange`, and `void` returns. Pass another registered object to an object argument with its generation-qualified handle, for example `@obj_0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef_43`. Struct arguments are explicit typed JSON, for example `'{"type":"CGPoint","x":12.5,"y":40}'` or `'{"type":"CGRect","x":0,"y":0,"width":320,"height":100}'`; struct returns use the same typed shape. Objective-C block parameters accept JSON `null` only, which is marshaled as a nil block; non-null blocks, pointers, arbitrary unrecognized structs, and other unsafe ABI types are rejected rather than guessed. Add `--pin-result` when an object/class return value must survive later requests; FlexUltra retains it before the invocation request finishes.

The `trace` family exposes bounded ObjSee message tracing inside the selected process. `trace start` requires at least one include selector: `--class`, `--method`, `--image`, or a `--pattern CLASS METHOD` pair; corresponding `--exclude-*` filters narrow the stream. ObjSee wildcard patterns are accepted. Only one trace session can run in a process at a time. Three independent bounds apply: `--max-events` is the retained in-memory ring capacity (default 500, clamped to 100–5000), `--max-total-events` stops the trace after observing a total number of events (default 5000, clamped to 1–50000), and `--max-duration-ms` stops it after a lifetime budget (default 30000 ms, clamped to 100–300000 ms). Filling only the retained ring discards the oldest events while `dropped`/`total_seen` continue to account for them. Reaching either total-event or duration budget stops the trace automatically. `trace events --after <sequence>` provides a stable cursor for incremental AI polling and can be combined with `--offset` and a per-read limit capped at 500. Stopping a trace preserves the captured status/events until the next trace begins.

Trace status includes `session_id`, `active`, `argument_detail`, all three configured budgets, `total_seen`, `recorded`, `dropped`, the exact filters, `started_at_unix_ms`, and `duration_ms`, plus first/last retained sequence numbers when events exist. A stopped trace also reports `stopped_at_unix_ms` and `stop_reason` (`explicit`, `max_duration`, or `max_total_events`). Each captured event has a monotonic `sequence`, class/method identity, class-vs-instance flag, thread/depth metadata, and best-effort image/signature/caller metadata. `--arguments none|basic|class` defaults to `none`; `basic` and `class` collect additional argument metadata and add tracing overhead, so AI clients should start with `none` and enable more detail only for a focused trace.

`ui find` performs a bounded breadth-first search over the live UIKit tree and can filter by class, visible text/title, accessibility identifier, and accessibility label. Find and snapshot entries also include a handle-free stable selector, inferred `role`, and semantic `actions`, so an AI can discover capabilities such as `scroll`, `select`, `set_text`, `set_value`, and `activate` without guessing from class names. `ui resolve` turns that selector back into a fresh live handle by preferring exact accessibility/text identity and using the recorded hierarchy path to disambiguate or recover when needed. `ui wait` reuses the live find filters and waits for a matching view to exist or disappear, with bounded timeout and polling controls. `ui activate`, `ui select`, `ui set-text`, `ui set-value`, and `ui scroll` accept either a registered process-scoped handle or a stable selector; selector targets are resolved immediately before the action, so find-once/act-later flows survive redraws and process relaunches when the selector still identifies the view. `ui deep-inspect` is the recommended one-shot investigation primitive for an AI that already has a live view/controller handle or stable selector. It combines root-relative UIKit state and a reusable stable selector with the owner controller, superview and responder chains, relevant constraints, layer metadata, gestures and target/actions, `UIControl` actions, accessibility state, defining Mach-O images, and bounded FLEX class/property/ivar/instance-method/class-method metadata. It accepts the same selector-resolution controls as the other selector-native operations, reports `target_source` and `resolved_by`, defaults each FLEX member collection to 60 entries, clamps the requested member limit to 1–200, and caps relationship/chains separately so a single investigation stays token-bounded. Use `--no-values` when class/member shape is enough. `ui select` gives list rows their own semantic action: selectable `UITableViewCell`/`UICollectionViewCell` snapshot entries advertise `select`, and the agent resolves the owning list plus index path before entering UIKit's user-selection path. This lets SwiftUI-backed Settings rows and conventional UIKit lists navigate without falling back to screen coordinates. `ui set-value` gives AI clients typed control semantics: switches require a JSON boolean, sliders and steppers require an in-range finite number, and segmented controls require an in-range integer segment index (including `-1` for no selection). It emits `UIControlEventValueChanged` by default; `--no-notify` performs a reversible visual/state update without the normal control callback, and `--animated` animates switch/slider updates when UIKit supports it. Snapshot entries for these controls expose `set_value` in `actions` plus their current `value` and relevant bounds/segment metadata. `ui hit-test` lets a visual agent map a screenshot coordinate to the exact live UIKit view under that point plus its ancestor chain, stable selectors, root-relative frames, and FLEX-compatible object handles without triggering an action. `ui tap` uses the same coordinate model as an action fallback: it hit-tests a root-relative point, walks up to the nearest actionable UIKit view, and reports whether it focused a text input, dispatched `UIControlEventTouchUpInside`, or used accessibility activation. It performs semantic UIKit activation after hit-testing rather than synthesizing a hardware touch. The broker-level physical-input family complements these semantic UIKit actions with real digitizer `tap`, `double-tap`, `long-press`, `swipe`, `drag`, `touch`, and `touch-sequence` operations through runtime-optional iCLI, without requiring an injected target. Raw touch operations can also use normalized 0–1 fixed-portrait digitizer coordinates. `ui first-responder` reports the currently focused UIKit view with a live handle and stable selector; `ui dismiss-keyboard` resigns focus and ends editing for the key window, and is an idempotent no-op when nothing is focused. `ui alert` inspects the currently presented `UIAlertController`, exposing its title/message, style, actions, preferred action, text fields, and live FLEX handles. `ui alert-action` chooses one action by exact title or zero-based index and activates the matching visible UIKit representation; when public activation paths refuse the event, it can use either the representation's direct interface-action entry point or the `UIInterfaceAction` owned by that visible representation, while still never calling the private `UIAlertAction` handler block directly. `ui back` first follows the effective UIKit controller hierarchy, then discovers nested visible `UINavigationController` instances through the live view/responder graph so SwiftUI navigation stacks can be popped directly. If a stack is not exposed, it can activate a visible upper-left `BackButton`/`Back` control and reports that fallback explicitly. Direct pops honor `--animated`; fallback control activation reports that animation is not directly controlled. `ui dismiss` dismisses the deepest presented controller. `ui screenshot` returns base64 JPEG/PNG data plus dimensions and metadata. `ui snapshot` combines a screenshot with a compact list of visible, meaningful UIKit elements, screen-relative frames, accessibility metadata, live handles, stable selectors, inferred roles, and semantic actions for AI clients. Pass `--no-image` when only the structured perception data is needed.

`runtime class` resolves an exact loaded Objective-C class into a normal FlexUltra object handle. That handle can be passed to the FLEX-backed object inspection tools and to `object call --class`, giving AI clients a direct class-search → class-inspect → class-method path without first locating an instance. `runtime class-protocols <exact>` maps that class to the protocols directly adopted by it and, by default, its superclass chain while preserving each declaring class. The runtime catalog also mirrors FLEX's loaded-image browser: `runtime images` returns image display names plus exact paths, `runtime image-classes` lists the Objective-C classes FLEX associates with one selected image, and `runtime protocols` browses loaded Objective-C protocols. `runtime protocol <exact>` turns one loaded protocol name into its directly adopted protocols plus bounded required/optional instance/class method contracts, including Objective-C type encodings and machine-readable argument/return types. `runtime protocol-classes <exact>` completes the reverse lookup by listing every currently loaded Objective-C class that conforms to the selected FLEX-catalog protocol, including inherited conformance, superclass name, and defining image path. `runtime methods [query] --class-name <exact> [--kind any|instance|class]` searches the selected loaded class through `FLEXRuntimeClient`, supports standard pagination, and returns the same machine-readable invocation metadata as `object methods` so an AI client can discover a selector before it has an instance handle. `runtime properties [query] --class-name <exact> [--kind any|instance|class]` and `runtime ivars [query] --class-name <exact>` use `FLEXObjectExplorer` to expose property and ivar metadata directly from a class. They intentionally omit live values, letting an AI map class state safely before it has an instance handle. These runtime catalog surfaces are also exposed through the matching `flexultra_runtime_*` MCP tools.

The `heap` family exposes FLEX heap discovery without leaking FLEX's internal `FLEXObjectRef` wrappers into the public object model. `heap snapshot` mirrors FLEX's Live Objects / Heap Objects discovery path and returns each live class with its instance count, `class_getInstanceSize` value, and estimated live bytes; `--query` filters class names and `--sort name|count|size` controls ordering. `heap instances <Class>` returns the live underlying objects as normal process-scoped handles; `heap subclasses <Class>` returns loaded subclass names; and `heap references <handle|selector-json>` finds live objects whose object/class ivars point at the target. `heap reference-graph <handle|selector-json>` builds a bounded, cycle-safe reverse-reference BFS whose edges point from each referrer to the object it references. Its root is depth 0; `--max-depth`, `--max-nodes`, and `--per-node-limit` default to 2, 100, and 50 and are capped at 5, 500, and 200. The response includes de-duplicated nodes, edges, traversal strategy, `heap_scans`, and truncation accounting so an AI can safely explore ownership/controller relationships without an unbounded heap walk. When FLEX supplies wrapper/reference context, FlexUltra preserves it separately as `flex_reference`. Heap enumeration defaults to `retained: false`; `--retained` is available when the caller deliberately wants FLEX to retain enumerated objects, but it is more invasive and can be unsafe for some classes. `heap subclasses` uses `FLEXRuntimeUtility` when the installed FLEX exposes the modern subclass API and otherwise uses an Objective-C runtime compatibility path. `heap references` and `heap reference-graph` use the cached ivar-layout scanner over `FLEXHeapEnumerator` when supported and fall back to FLEX's default reverse-reference implementation when necessary. Optimized `heap reference-graph` traversal performs one full heap pass per BFS depth; the compatibility fallback may still scan once per target. `heap snapshot`, `heap instances`, `heap references`, and `heap reference-graph` run on a dedicated per-target heap worker so long malloc-zone scans do not block ordinary UI/runtime/object requests. Only one heap enumeration may run at a time in a target; overlapping requests fail immediately with `heap_busy`. Heap operations are materially slower than ordinary inspection, so CLI and MCP requests whose operation starts with `heap.` use a longer response timeout. AI clients can call these through the matching `flexultra_heap_*` MCP tools, including `flexultra_heap_reference_graph`.

The `bookmarks` family mirrors FLEX's process-local `FLEXBookmarkManager`. `bookmarks list` returns bookmark array order, original zero-based indices, and live FlexUltra object references; optional `--query`, `--offset`, and `--limit` make the list AI-friendly without changing the underlying indices. `bookmarks add` accepts either a live handle or the same stable UIKit selector JSON used by other selector-native operations, and `bookmarks remove` deletes exactly one current array index. Bookmark mutations affect only the target process and can be reversed by removing the returned index.

`network transactions` exposes FLEX's in-process network recorder without opening the FLEX UI. It defaults to HTTP and also supports `--kind websocket` and `--kind firebase`, plus server-side `--query`, `--offset`, and `--limit`. An empty `transactions` array is a valid result when the target has not recorded traffic. Each returned transaction is a normal live FlexUltra object handle with compact FLEX descriptions, timing/state/received-byte metadata, and an optional error handle, so an AI client can immediately continue with `object inspect`, `object properties`, `object methods`, or `object call` for deeper analysis. The response also returns a live `recorder` handle and both `total` (after query filtering) and `recorded_total` (before filtering).

`logs messages` exposes FLEX's OS log controller without presenting the FLEX system-log UI. FlexUltra enables persistent capture, starts monitoring, then snapshots the controller's current message history on the main queue before filtering or paging it, so asynchronous FLEX log updates cannot mutate the collection during enumeration. Optional `--query` matches the verified FLEX `sender` and `messageText` fields case-insensitively; `--offset` and `--limit` use the standard pagination contract. Each message is returned as a live FlexUltra object handle plus `date`, `sender`, `message_text`, and `message_id`. An empty `messages` array is a valid result, which is expected immediately after monitoring begins in a quiet or freshly launched process.

The `defaults` family exposes UserDefaults in a form suitable for automation. `defaults entries` uses FLEX's `FLEXDefaultsContentSection`: by default it mirrors FLEX's app-owned preference scope, while `--include-registered` exposes the full `NSUserDefaults.standardUserDefaults` `dictionaryRepresentation`. `--query`, `--offset`, and `--limit` filter and page entries before returning them. `defaults get`, `defaults set`, and `defaults remove` operate directly on `standardUserDefaults`. `defaults set` accepts JSON strings, booleans, numbers, arrays, and dictionaries that are valid property-list values; JSON `null` is intentionally rejected so deletion remains explicit through `defaults remove`. Native `NSDate` and `NSData` values encountered while reading are represented as tagged JSON objects.

The `experiment` family gives AI clients a bounded way to try reversible mutations and then either keep or undo them. An experiment is tied to the current injected process generation, only one can be active per target process, and it records at most 256 mutations. The v1 reversible set is `defaults set`, `defaults remove`, `ui set-text`, `ui set-value`, and `ui scroll`; pass `--experiment <experiment_id>` to opt an individual supported mutation into the active session. `experiment rollback` restores recorded state in reverse order and suppresses normal UI callbacks where possible, while `experiment commit` discards the undo log and keeps the changes. Errors distinguish an already-active session, no active session, a stale process generation, a mismatched ID, busy bookkeeping, and a full undo log. If bookkeeping fails after a mutation has already happened, FlexUltra immediately attempts to restore the captured state and reports `mutation_reverted` plus `revert_error` if that restoration also fails. `object set` and other mutating operations are outside the v1 reversible set.

The `keychain` family is read-only and FLEX-backed. `keychain items` enumerates generic-password records that the injected target process can access through `FLEXKeychain`; it does not represent the device-wide Keychain. Results are sorted by service, account, access group, and label, then filtered/paginated with the optional query, offset, and limit. `keychain item <service> <account>` resolves an exact item and uses `FLEXKeychainQuery` to fetch its password data. Add `--access-group` when the same service/account pair appears in multiple access groups; otherwise an ambiguous match is rejected. Password data is returned as UTF-8 when valid and base64 otherwise. FlexUltra exposes no Keychain mutation operation.

The `database sqlite` family exposes FLEX's `FLEXSQLiteDatabaseManager` without exposing arbitrary SQL. `tables` enumerates table names, `columns` resolves the columns for one exact table, and `rows` returns a paginated page of FLEX-normalized row values. Database files must be regular files addressed by relative paths inside the same confined `home` or `bundle` roots as the filesystem API; traversal and symlink escapes are rejected. Table names must first exist in FLEX's table enumeration, and FlexUltra exposes no execute/update/insert/delete endpoint.

The `database realm` family exposes the matching read-only inspection surface from `FLEXRealmDatabaseManager`: `tables`, `columns`, and bounded `rows`. It uses the same confined relative `home`/`bundle` paths and exact table-name validation. Realm values are converted to JSON-safe values for AI/MCP use; non-scalar Realm-linked objects are returned through FlexUltra's normal live object references so they can be inspected further. The target app must actually load Realm's Objective-C runtime (`RLMRealm`); otherwise the operation returns `realm_unavailable`. FlexUltra exposes no Realm mutation operation.

The `filesystem` family provides bounded, read-only app filesystem inspection. Its default `home` root is the target process's `NSHomeDirectory()` app container; `--root bundle` switches to the main application bundle. Paths are relative to the selected root, normalized before access, and rejected if traversal or symlink resolution would escape that root. `filesystem list` and `filesystem search` are paginated. `filesystem read` returns UTF-8 text when possible and base64 otherwise, reads at most 64 KiB by default, and has a hard 1 MiB cap. Recursive search matches filename substrings case-insensitively in deterministic path order, does not follow symlink directories, is bounded by `--max-nodes` and `--max-depth`, and reports both traversal truncation and unreadable-directory counts. Filesystem operations are inspection-only.

Object handles use the form `obj_<generation>_<counter>`, for example `obj_0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef_42`. The generation is a per-process opaque identifier, so handles are scoped to one injected process lifetime and held weakly by default. A handle from a previous process generation returns `stale_handle` with `handle_generation` and `current_generation`; an unknown or deallocated handle from the current generation returns `object_not_found`. They can also expire when the app releases the underlying object. `object pin` intentionally retains an existing handle (or a selector-resolved object) across requests; `object unpin` releases that retention. Factory-style `object call` workflows should use `--pin-result` because a newly returned autoreleased object may otherwise disappear before a later standalone pin request. Stable selectors are handle-free and address-free, so they can be reused after redraws or a target relaunch when they still identify the intended UIKit object. AI clients should also pass the discovery generation as `expected_generation` on routed calls; `target_generation_changed` forces rediscovery before stale process-scoped state can be used against a replacement process. Addresses in JSON are debugging metadata only and are never accepted as object identifiers.

## MCP

`flexultra-mcp` speaks MCP over stdin/stdout. Its MCP `initialize` response includes server instructions that teach an AI client the preferred workflow: call `flexultra_targets`, consult `flexultra_target_history` when a requested target is missing or stale, prefer a target whose `build_status` is `current`, call `flexultra_target_resolve` when a bundle identifier or process name could be ambiguous and then use the returned PID, retain the returned `generation`, pass it as `expected_generation` to `flexultra_target_health` and every later injected-target call, then use `flexultra_investigate_screen`, follow with `flexultra_investigate_element` for the selected tweak target, and expand with focused UI/object/Swift/runtime/heap/trace tools as needed. Every failed request exposes the same machine-readable recovery fields: `category`, `retryable`, `recovery_hint`, `recommended_action`, and `suggested_operations`, while preserving operation-specific error metadata. AI clients should perform the recommended recovery before retrying and should not blindly repeat an unchanged request when `retryable` is false. Every tool also publishes standard MCP annotations (`readOnlyHint`, `destructiveHint`, `idempotentHint`, and `openWorldHint`) so an agent can distinguish passive inspection from state-changing or potentially externally consequential operations before calling them. `flexultra_target_history` is a daemon-local read-only view of bounded connection metadata and provides evidence-based recovery hints without retaining app payloads or object handles; SpringBoard guidance never recommends a respring solely for diagnostics. `flexultra_target_resolve` requires only `target` and provides deterministic broker-side target selection. `flexultra_target_health` is the low-cost target qualification tool; it requires `target` and accepts optional `expected_generation` to pin the discovered process generation. `flexultra_investigate_screen` is the recommended first full AI inspection call after health passes because it combines screen perception, an automatically chosen or explicit focus, focused UIKit + FLEX metadata, optional Swift/Reflex metadata, and suggested follow-up actions. `flexultra_investigate_element` then collects the focused object's tweak-development evidence in one structured-only result. `flexultra_ui_snapshot_save` and `flexultra_ui_snapshot_diff` expose the generation-scoped, bounded UI baseline workflow to MCP clients, and `flexultra_ui_deep_inspect` remains available when the client wants only the focused UIKit/FLEX section. A desktop AI client can run the MCP server through the same SSH alias used for device administration:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "flexultra": {
      "command": "ssh",
      "args": ["26.0", "/var/jb/usr/bin/flexultra-mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

Run `python3 scripts/ai_agent_setup.py --host 26.0 --target com.apple.springboard --pretty` for a read-only MCP/target readiness check and a generated MCP configuration before handing the device to another agent. The doctor verifies the installed CLI/MCP executables, performs a real MCP `initialize` + `tools/list` handshake, confirms the native shared `ai_bootstrap_tools` minimum is present, and compares the complete live tool metadata against the compiled shared catalog, including descriptions, schemas, safety annotations, and duplicate registrations. It sends a read-only `flexultra_targets` call through MCP to `flexultrad`, requires a current injected target, then executes `flexultra_target_health` through MCP with the discovered generation pinned as `expected_generation`, and verifies that a deliberately stale generation is rejected with the structured `target_generation_changed` recovery contract. Missing or stale targets also produce `flexultra_target_history` lifecycle evidence with the daemon's recovery hint/action. `ready: true` therefore proves live MCP routing into a current agent with matching generation/build plus FLEX and UIKit health; full-catalog compatibility is reported separately so the intentionally smaller bootstrap minimum remains stable. Without `--target`, the doctor makes a best-effort `app.frontmost` lookup, then health-probes current targets in priority order: a matching frontmost app first, SpringBoard second, and all remaining current targets by broker recency. Health remains authoritative; the report records `target_selection: prioritized_first_healthy_current`, the winning `target_selection_reason`, and every attempted candidate. It reports `no_targets`, `no_current_targets`, or `no_healthy_current_targets` instead of treating MCP transport or build freshness alone as AI readiness. See `docs/AI_AGENT_GUIDE.md` for the complete AI workflow and a reusable onboarding prompt.

The MCP server exposes app list/running/frontmost/launch/kill, the full physical input family (`tap`, `double-tap`, `long-press`, `swipe`, `drag`, `touch`, and `touch-sequence`), target discovery/lifecycle/resolution/qualification through `flexultra_targets`, `flexultra_target_history`, `flexultra_target_resolve`, and `flexultra_target_health`, FLEX status/show/hide, reversible experiment lifecycle through `flexultra_experiment_begin` / `flexultra_experiment_status` / `flexultra_experiment_rollback` / `flexultra_experiment_commit`, bounded ObjSee tracing through `flexultra_trace_start` / `flexultra_trace_status` / `flexultra_trace_events` / `flexultra_trace_stop`, runtime class search/resolution plus loaded-image/class/protocol catalog browsing, heap snapshot/instance/subclass/reverse-reference discovery, FLEX bookmark list/add/remove, FLEX network recorder history, FLEX OS log history, FLEX globals, structured UserDefaults inspection/mutation, read-only FLEX Keychain inspection, bounded read-only filesystem inspection, UIKit window/hierarchy/find/resolve/wait/activate/hit-test/tap/first-responder/dismiss-keyboard/back/dismiss/text/value/scroll/screenshot/snapshot operations, the aggregate `flexultra_investigate_screen` and `flexultra_investigate_element` investigation tools, metadata-only Swift inspection through `flexultra_swift_inspect`, and the complete focused object inspection/get/set/call surface. The reversible MCP mutation tools `flexultra_defaults_set`, `flexultra_defaults_remove`, `flexultra_ui_set_text`, `flexultra_ui_set_value`, and `flexultra_ui_scroll` accept optional `experiment_id`; the four lifecycle tools require only `target`. Physical input, UI activation, `object.set`, `object.call`, app lifecycle, and arbitrary FLEX globals are outside that rollback boundary, and the MCP instructions call this out explicitly. Screenshot, image-enabled snapshot, and image-enabled `investigate.screen` results include one MCP `image` content item while `structuredContent` keeps only JSON-friendly metadata. `investigate.screen` also removes `data` and `mime_type` from its nested snapshot to avoid duplicating the screenshot payload; `investigate.element` never emits image content.

## Installed-device smoke test

The smoke runner relaunches Settings by default, waits for a fresh agent, exercises the CLI and MCP server, validates screenshots, verifies ObjSee capture plus repeated start/stop session lifetime, and restores every alpha/text/scroll mutation before exiting:

```sh
python3 scripts/device_smoke.py --host 26.0 --target com.apple.Preferences
```

Use `--no-relaunch` to keep the current process, or `--screenshot-out /tmp/flexultra-smoke.jpg` to retain the decoded CLI screenshot.

For repeatable deployment across the required device matrix, use `python3 scripts/deploy_required_devices.py --pretty`. The deployer targets the `26.0`, `16.7.16`, and `16.3.1` SSH aliases by default, verifies that each alias reports the expected iOS version, rejects packages with an external `libflex` dependency, requires the packaged private FLEX runtime, refuses a package whose embedded agent build fingerprint does not match the current source tree, copies and installs the current `.theos/last_package`, verifies the installed package plus private FLEX runtime and agent file, and restarts only `flexultrad`. After the broker restart it gives long-running agents a bounded window to register again before SpringBoard qualification. It never invokes APT, never bypasses repository authentication, and never restarts SpringBoard. A long-running SpringBoard that still has an older injected agent is reported as `deployed_springboard_stale`; a SpringBoard that does not re-register within the bounded window is reported as `deployed_target_not_registered`. Package deployment remains distinguishable from loaded-agent qualification. Add `--run-smoke` to run the reversible Settings smoke suite only when iCLI does not report the device locked.

For read-only SpringBoard qualification, use `python3 scripts/springboard_qualify.py --host 26.0 --pretty`. It checks target discovery/health, ping/info, FLEX, UIKit windows, a harmless `UIView` runtime lookup, bounded image-free screen investigation, focused deep inspection, and the Swift metadata-only safety contract when `target.health.capabilities.swift_inspection` is true. Qualification requires Swift values to remain disabled and verifies the value-request suppression path as well as `swift_mirror=false` and `reflex=false`. It never restarts SpringBoard and never invokes a UI mutation. JSON goes to stdout and the concise status summary goes to stderr; UI/key-window limitations are reported separately from injection/FLEX failures. The qualifier computes the expected deterministic agent source fingerprint and compares it with the injected target's `agent_build` in addition to checking required capabilities. If the installed package was updated while SpringBoard stayed alive, the script reports `stale_agent` plus `refresh_required: true` even when an older agent exposes the same operation list. That is distinct from broken injection: the target must be restarted at an appropriate time before current-version qualification can pass.

`python3 scripts/compatibility_report.py --pretty` collects the same proof across the required `26.0`, `16.7.16`, and `16.3.1` aliases, including FlexUltra package state, the packaged private FLEX runtime, daemon reachability, SpringBoard discovery, loaded-agent freshness, target health, and read-only SpringBoard qualification. The command exits nonzero unless every requested host passes every requested gate, so an unreachable required device, failed interactive suite, or locked device that blocks a requested interactive suite cannot silently pass a release gate. Add `--run-smoke` to run the reversible Settings feature smoke suite with `--skip-keychain-content`, and add `--run-soak` to run the Settings reliability suite covering broker reconnects, repeated CLI/MCP polling, ObjSee trace lifetime, heap timeout recovery, and stale-handle/stable-selector behavior across relaunches. When either interactive suite is requested and iCLI is available, the reporter checks device lock state first and records `blocked_ui` without launching Settings on a locked device. Release automation can additionally opt into `--refresh-stale-springboard` when SpringBoard is registered with a stale agent or when a live SpringBoard is missing from the broker after a daemon restart. Before changing state, the reporter identifies the actual live SpringBoard PID on-device and, when the broker has a SpringBoard record, requires its advertised PID to match; ambiguous discovery or a broker/live PID mismatch is refused. It sends `SIGTERM` only to that verified PID, waits for a different SpringBoard process to register the current deterministic agent build plus `target.health`, and then reruns the normal read-only qualifier. The refresh is explicit and never runs during normal qualification.

`python3 scripts/qualification_report.py --pretty` is the top-level qualification command for handoff or release work. It keeps three gates separate in one JSON result: local source/package/protocol checks, multi-device SpringBoard compatibility, and live MCP AI readiness. The AI gate defaults to the `26.0` device and, when no explicit target is supplied, chooses the first healthy target after prioritizing the frontmost injected app, SpringBoard, then remaining current targets by recency. Pass `--ai-target com.apple.springboard` when SpringBoard itself must be the AI-ready target. The compatibility gate still covers all three required aliases by default, so a dependency-blocked device remains visibly different from a local regression failure or a live MCP readiness failure. Add `--run-smoke` for the reversible Settings feature suite and `--run-soak` for the longer reliability suite; when requested, those results participate in the compatibility gate instead of being informational only. `--refresh-stale-springboard` passes the same explicit verified-PID recovery policy through to compatibility qualification for either a stale registered SpringBoard or a live SpringBoard missing from the broker.

See `docs/PROTOCOL.md` for the broker protocol and MCP mapping.
